claim: You should put butter on a burn to help it heal.
explanation: Butter, oil, or toothpaste trap heat in the burn and can cause infection. Cool running water is the safe first step.
whyItMatters: Using the wrong home remedy can turn a small burn into a worse injury.

claim: If you pick food up within 5 seconds, it is safe to eat.
explanation: Bacteria can transfer to food almost instantly. The 5-second rule is not a real safety rule.
whyItMatters: Foodborne germs can cause stomach upset and more serious illness.

explanation: Studies do not show that sugar causes hyperactivity. Excitement at parties and expectations often explain the behaviour.
whyItMatters: Blaming sugar can hide other reasons for behaviour and lead to unnecessary restrictions.

explanation: The pop is gas bubbles in the joint fluid. Research has not found a link between knuckle cracking and arthritis.
whyItMatters: Knowing the real cause helps you judge health claims instead of fearing normal body sounds.

claim: You must wait an hour after eating before swimming.
explanation: There is no evidence that swimming after eating is dangerous. Avoid very large meals right before hard exercise, but normal eating is fine.
whyItMatters: Old rules can stop people enjoying safe activity.

claim: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker and darker.
explanation: Shaving cuts hair at the surface. It does not change the root, so regrowth is not thicker. Short hair can simply feel coarser.
whyItMatters: This myth causes unnecessary worry about normal grooming.

claim: Humans only use 10% of their brains.
explanation: Brain scans show that people use virtually all of their brain, with different areas active for different tasks.
whyItMatters: The 10% myth can be used to sell fake 'brain training' products.

claim: Being cold or wet gives you a cold.
explanation: Colds are caused by viruses, not by cold weather. Cold weather may keep people indoors where viruses spread more easily.
whyItMatters: Knowing the real cause helps you focus on handwashing and rest.

claim: Vitamin C prevents colds in most people.
explanation: For most people, vitamin C does not prevent colds. It may slightly shorten a cold in some cases, but it is not a shield.
whyItMatters: Relying on supplements can distract from proven habits like sleep and hand hygiene.
source: Cochrane Review — Vitamin C and colds

explanation: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only fight bacteria. Using them unnecessarily can cause resistance.
whyItMatters: Antibiotic resistance is a serious global health problem.

claim: Washing hands with soap reduces the spread of many infections.
explanation: Soap and water remove germs from your hands. It is one of the simplest and most effective health habits.
whyItMatters: Handwashing protects you and the people around you, at school and at home.

claim: Wearing a seatbelt lowers the risk of serious injury in a crash.
explanation: Seatbelts stop your body from moving forward violently and spread the force across stronger parts of the body.
whyItMatters: Seatbelts save lives, even on short trips.
